## Proof

Let $R = \mathbb{C}[X_1,\dots,X_n]$. For a point $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in \mathbb{A}^n(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}^n$, the **evaluation homomorphism** is
$$\operatorname{ev}_a : R \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}, \qquad \operatorname{ev}_a(f)=f(a_1,\dots,a_n).$$
This is a ring homomorphism, and in fact a **$\mathbb{C}$-algebra** homomorphism, since for every $c\in\mathbb{C}$,
$$\operatorname{ev}_a(c)=c,$$
i.e. $\operatorname{ev}_a$ fixes $\mathbb{C}$ pointwise.

The question asks whether the map
$$\Phi:\mathbb{A}^n(\mathbb{C})\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(R,\mathbb{C}),\qquad a\longmapsto \operatorname{ev}_a$$
is **surjective onto the set of all ring homomorphisms** $R\to\mathbb{C}$.

### The answer is **No**.

The key observation is that a ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to\mathbb{C}$ need not fix $\mathbb{C}$ pointwise. Its restriction $\varphi|_{\mathbb{C}}:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a ring endomorphism of $\mathbb{C}$, and there exist nontrivial ring automorphisms of $\mathbb{C}$.

**Explicit counterexample.** Let $\sigma:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be complex conjugation, $\sigma(z)=\bar z$. This is a ring automorphism of $\mathbb{C}$ (it preserves addition, multiplication, and $1$), but it is **not** the identity: $\sigma(i)=-i\neq i$.

Let $\operatorname{ev}_0:R\to\mathbb{C}$ be evaluation at the origin $0=(0,\dots,0)$, and define
$$\varphi := \sigma\circ \operatorname{ev}_0 : R \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}.$$
As a composition of ring homomorphisms, $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism.

**Claim:** $\varphi$ is not an evaluation homomorphism.

Indeed, for any $c\in\mathbb{C}$ viewed as a constant polynomial,
$$\varphi(c)=\sigma(\operatorname{ev}_0(c))=\sigma(c)=\bar c.$$
In particular $\varphi(i)=\overline{i}=-i$.

On the other hand, every evaluation homomorphism $\operatorname{ev}_a$ fixes $\mathbb{C}$ pointwise:
$$\operatorname{ev}_a(c)=c \quad\text{for all } c\in\mathbb{C},$$
so in particular $\operatorname{ev}_a(i)=i$ for every $a\in\mathbb{C}^n$.

Since $\varphi(i)=-i\neq i=\operatorname{ev}_a(i)$ for every $a$, the homomorphism $\varphi$ is not in the image of $\Phi$. Hence $\Phi$ is **not surjective**.

### Remark (the $\mathbb{C}$-algebra case)

If instead one considers the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}\text{-}\mathbf{alg}}(R,\mathbb{C})$ of $\mathbb{C}$-algebra homomorphisms (ring homomorphisms that fix $\mathbb{C}$ pointwise), then $\Phi$ **is** bijective. A $\mathbb{C}$-algebra homomorphism $\psi:R\to\mathbb{C}$ is completely determined by the values $b_i=\psi(X_i)\in\mathbb{C}$, and then $\psi=\operatorname{ev}_{(b_1,\dots,b_n)}$. Thus
$$\Phi:\mathbb{A}^n(\mathbb{C})\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}\text{-}\mathbf{alg}}(R,\mathbb{C})$$
is an isomorphism. The failure of surjectivity is therefore entirely due to the existence of nontrivial ring automorphisms of $\mathbb{C}$ (such as conjugation, and in fact many others, since $\mathbb{C}$ has $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ automorphisms as a field).

### Conclusion

The evaluation homomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb{A}^n(\mathbb{C})\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(\mathbb{C}[X_1,\dots,X_n],\mathbb{C})$ is **not surjective**, because composing evaluation with a nontrivial ring automorphism of $\mathbb{C}$ (e.g. complex conjugation) yields a ring homomorphism that does not fix $\mathbb{C}$ and hence cannot be any evaluation map.

### PROOF COMPLETE
